## Overview

This document pulls together the headline results of the spatial ATE analysis: trial-level sample composition, department-level mortality and ATE summaries with heterogeneity tests, model comparison statistics and Matérn correlation ranges, the predicted mortality and ATE surfaces from the spatial models, the posterior probability map of a beneficial ATE, and the CSI-level comparison.

It is a reporting layer. Everything it shows was computed in `01`–`04` and is read back from `data/`; the two exceptions are the department-level heterogeneity tests and the summary tables, which are computed inline.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
rm(list = ls())
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide

source(here::here("analysis", "0-config.R"))
source(here::here("analysis", "0-functions.R"))

df_all <- readRDS(here("data","grappe_mortality_data.rds"))

dist_summ <- readRDS(here("data", "district_ATE_means.rds"))

ate_preds <- readRDS(here("data", "preds_ATE.rds")) 
post_prob_raw <- readRDS(here("data", "post_prob_dat.rds"))

aics <- readRDS(here("data", "model_aic_table.rds"))
lrts <- readRDS(here("data", "model_lrt_table.rds"))

csi_dat <- readRDS(here("data", "csi_dat.rds"))
csi_preds <- readRDS(here("data", "csi_preds_mort.rds"))

fit_simp_krig    <- readRDS(here("data", "fitmort_child_simp_krig.rds"))
fit_gen_krig     <- readRDS(here("data", "fitmort_child_gen_krig.rds"))
fit_gen_krig_int <- readRDS(here("data", "fitmort_child_gen_krig_int.rds"))

fit_csi_simp_krig    <- readRDS(here("data", "fit_csi_simp_krig.rds"))
fit_csi_gen_krig <- readRDS(here("data", "fit_csi_gen_krig.rds"))

niger_adm1 <- st_read(dsn = here("data", "untouched", "ner_admin_boundaries", "ner_admin1.shp"))
niger_adm2 <- st_read(dsn = here("data", "untouched", "ner_admin_boundaries", "ner_admin2.shp"))

niger_adm2_sub <- readRDS(here("data", "niger_adm2_sub.rds"))
niger_adm2_sub_proj <- niger_adm2_sub %>%
  st_transform(crs = proj_crs)
```

```{r}
#| label: data-preprocessing
#| include: true

districts <- df_all %>% distinct(district) %>% pull(district)

# Multiple grappes can have the same name and be in different districts, so we can't use grappe as a unique identifier for merging with the spatial data. Use site_code instead.
# grappes <- df_all %>% distinct(grappe) %>% pull(grappe) 

df_proj <- df_all %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = global_crs) %>%
  st_transform(crs = proj_crs) %>%
  mutate(lon = sf::st_coordinates(.)[,1],
         lat = sf::st_coordinates(.)[,2])

dist_summ <- dist_summ %>%
  dplyr::filter(district %in% districts)

```

```{r}
#| label: precompute-stats
#| include: true

# sample composition
n_grappes_total     <- nrow(df_all)
n_grappes_child_az  <- sum(df_all$tx == "Child Azithro")
n_grappes_infant_az <- sum(df_all$tx == "Infant Azithro")
n_grappes_placebo   <- sum(df_all$tx == "Placebo")
n_grappes_treatment <- sum(df_all$isTreated_child == "Treatment")
n_grappes_control   <- sum(df_all$isTreated_child == "Control")

n_csis              <- nrow(csi_dat)
grappes_per_csi_vec <- df_all %>% dplyr::count(csi) %>% pull(n)
grappe_per_csi_med  <- median(grappes_per_csi_vec)
grappe_per_csi_min  <- min(grappes_per_csi_vec)
grappe_per_csi_max  <- max(grappes_per_csi_vec)

# person-time and deaths
total_pt         <- sum(df_all$pt_year_1to59)
pt_treatment     <- sum(df_all$pt_year_1to59[df_all$isTreated_child == "Treatment"])
pt_control       <- sum(df_all$pt_year_1to59[df_all$isTreated_child == "Control"])
total_deaths     <- sum(df_all$n_deaths_1to59)
deaths_treatment <- sum(df_all$n_deaths_1to59[df_all$isTreated_child == "Treatment"])
deaths_control   <- sum(df_all$n_deaths_1to59[df_all$isTreated_child == "Control"])
overall_rate     <- total_deaths / total_pt * 1000
rate_treatment   <- deaths_treatment / pt_treatment * 1000
rate_control     <- deaths_control / pt_control * 1000
overall_ate      <- rate_treatment - rate_control

# department-level lookup vectors (district name → value)
dept_grappes   <- df_all   %>% dplyr::count(district, name = "n_grappes")    %>% tibble::deframe()
dept_ate       <- dist_summ %>% dplyr::select(district, ATE)                 %>% tibble::deframe()
dept_mort_ctrl <- dist_summ %>% dplyr::select(district, MortRate_Control)     %>% tibble::deframe()
dept_mort_trt  <- dist_summ %>% dplyr::select(district, MortRate_Treatment)   %>% tibble::deframe()

# Matern parameters
.rho_to_km <- function(fit) 1 / (1000 * fit$CorrEst_and_RanFix$corrPars$`1`$rho)
.get_rho   <- function(fit) fit$CorrEst_and_RanFix$corrPars$`1`$rho
.get_nu    <- function(fit) fit$CorrEst_and_RanFix$corrPars$`1`$nu

rho_csi_simp <- .get_rho(fit_csi_simp_krig)
rho_csi_gen  <- .get_rho(fit_csi_gen_krig)

range_simp_km    <- .rho_to_km(fit_simp_krig)
range_gen_km     <- .rho_to_km(fit_gen_krig)
range_gen_int_km <- .rho_to_km(fit_gen_krig_int)

range_csi_simp_km    <- .rho_to_km(fit_csi_simp_krig)
range_csi_gen_km     <- .rho_to_km(fit_csi_gen_krig)

nu_simp_krig    <- .get_nu(fit_simp_krig)
nu_gen_krig     <- .get_nu(fit_gen_krig)
nu_gen_krig_int <- .get_nu(fit_gen_krig_int)

nu_csi_simp_krig <- .get_nu(fit_csi_simp_krig)
nu_csi_gen_krig <- .get_nu(fit_csi_gen_krig)

lambda_gen_int <- fit_gen_krig_int$lambda[["lon + lat"]]

# model selection stats from pre-computed tables
aic_simp    <- aics %>% dplyr::filter(grepl("Simple",            Model)) %>% dplyr::pull(AIC)
aic_gen     <- aics %>% dplyr::filter(Model == "Generalized Kriging")    %>% dplyr::pull(AIC)
aic_gen_int <- aics %>% dplyr::filter(grepl("Interaction",       Model)) %>% dplyr::pull(AIC)
aic_gen_re  <- aics %>% dplyr::filter(grepl("Cluster",           Model)) %>% dplyr::pull(AIC)

aic_csi_simp <- AIC(fit_csi_simp_krig)[1]
aic_csi_gen  <- AIC(fit_csi_gen_krig)[1]

lrt_gen_vs_simp_stat <- lrts %>% dplyr::filter(grepl("Simple",      Comparison)) %>% dplyr::pull(LRT_statistic)
lrt_gen_vs_simp_p    <- lrts %>% dplyr::filter(grepl("Simple",      Comparison)) %>% dplyr::pull(p_value)
lrt_int_vs_gen_stat  <- lrts %>% dplyr::filter(grepl("Interaction", Comparison)) %>% dplyr::pull(LRT_statistic)
lrt_int_vs_gen_p     <- lrts %>% dplyr::filter(grepl("Interaction", Comparison)) %>% dplyr::pull(p_value)

# lrt_csi <- spaMM::LRT(fit_csi_gen_krig, fit_csi_simp_krig)$basicLRT

# CSI stats
csi_med_deaths <- median(csi_dat$n_deaths_1to59)
csi_min_deaths <- min(csi_dat$n_deaths_1to59)
csi_max_deaths <- max(csi_dat$n_deaths_1to59)
csi_med_pt     <- round(median(csi_dat$pt_year_1to59))
csi_min_pt     <- round(min(csi_dat$pt_year_1to59))
csi_max_pt     <- round(max(csi_dat$pt_year_1to59))
```

# Trial data and outcomes

The analytic sample comprised `r n_grappes_total`^★^ grappes: `r n_grappes_child_az`^★^ in the azithromycin 1–59 months arm, `r n_grappes_infant_az`^★^ in the azithromycin infants arm, and `r n_grappes_placebo`^★^ in the placebo arm. After pooling the infant azithromycin and placebo arms into a single control group, `r n_grappes_treatment`^★^ grappes were assigned to the treatment group and `r n_grappes_control`^★^ to the control group. Grappes were aggregated to `r n_csis`^★^ CSIs (median `r grappe_per_csi_med`^★^ grappes per CSI; range `r grappe_per_csi_min`–`r grappe_per_csi_max`^★^).

Total follow-up was `r scales::comma(round(total_pt))`^★^ child-years (`r scales::comma(round(pt_treatment))`^★^ treatment; `r scales::comma(round(pt_control))`^★^ control). There were `r scales::comma(total_deaths)`^★^ deaths overall (`r deaths_treatment`^★^ treatment; `r deaths_control`^★^ control), yielding an overall mortality rate of `r round(overall_rate, 1)`^★^ deaths per 1,000 person-years (`r round(rate_treatment, 1)`^★^ treatment; `r round(rate_control, 1)`^★^ control). The crude rate difference (treatment minus control) was `r round(overall_ate, 1)`^★^ deaths per 1,000 person-years.

```{r}
  labs(x = "Person-years of follow-up", y = "Number of grappes") +
  theme_minimal() +
  ylim(c(0, 350))

hist2 <- ggplot(data = df_all) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = n_deaths_1to59), bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Number of deaths (1-59 months)", y = "Number of grappes") +
  theme_minimal() +
  ylim(c(0, 350)) +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_blank())

hist3 <- ggplot(data = df_all) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = deaths_per_1000_1to59), bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Mortality rate (deaths per 1000 py)", y = "Number of grappes") +
  theme_minimal() +

hist1 | hist2 | hist3
```

## Relationships between mortality outcomes and person-time, by treatment group

```{r}
#| label: par-coords-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

par_coords_dat <- df_all %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  dplyr::select(isTreated_child, pt_year_1to59, n_deaths_1to59, deaths_per_1000_1to59) %>%
  mutate(row_n = row_number()) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(deaths_per_1000_1to59, n_deaths_1to59), 
               names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
   mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = c("n_deaths_1to59", "deaths_per_1000_1to59"),
                            labels = c("# deaths", "deaths per 1000 py")))

mort_par <- ggplot(data = par_coords_dat) +
  geom_point(aes(x = variable, y = value, color = pt_year_1to59), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(x = variable, y = value, group = row_n, color = pt_year_1to59), alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~isTreated_child, nrow = 2) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Person-years", option = "D", direction = -1, limits = c(0, 800)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        axis.title.x = element_blank())

mort_dot <- ggplot(data = df_all, aes(x = n_deaths_1to59, y = deaths_per_1000_1to59)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = pt_year_1to59), alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Person-years", option = "D", direction = -1, limits = c(0, 800)) +
  facet_wrap(~isTreated_child, nrow = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(x = "Total deaths", y = "Deaths per 1000 person-years") +
  stat_cor(method = "pearson", 
           label.x = 30, label.y = 10, hjust = 1, vjust = 0,
           size = 4)

mort_par | mort_dot +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```

## department-level summaries of mortality outcomes and ATE

```{r}
#| label: department-names-map

base_map +
  geom_text(data = niger_adm2_sub, aes(x = st_coordinates(st_centroid(geometry))[,1], 
                      y = st_coordinates(st_centroid(geometry))[,2], 
                      label = adm2_name), size = 3)

```

The `r length(dept_grappes)`^★^ departments in the study area had between `r min(dept_grappes)`^★^ (Falmey) and `r max(dept_grappes)`^★^ (Dosso) grappes each (Boboye: `r dept_grappes[["Boboye"]]`^★^; Dioundiou: `r dept_grappes[["Dioundiou"]]`^★^; Dogondoutchi: `r dept_grappes[["Dogondoutchi"]]`^★^; Dosso: `r dept_grappes[["Dosso"]]`^★^; Falmey: `r dept_grappes[["Falmey"]]`^★^; Gaya: `r dept_grappes[["Gaya"]]`^★^; Loga: `r dept_grappes[["Loga"]]`^★^; Tibiri: `r dept_grappes[["Tibiri"]]`^★^).

### Test of heterogeneity in mortality rates across departments

```{r}
#| label: heterogeneity-test-mort

global_poi_mod <- glm(n_deaths_1to59 ~ isTreated_child + offset(log(pt_year_1to59)),
                      data = subset(df_all, pt_year_1to59 > 0), family = poisson(link = "log"))

state_poi_mod <- glm(n_deaths_1to59 ~ isTreated_child + factor(district) + offset(log(pt_year_1to59)),
                      data = subset(df_all, pt_year_1to59 > 0), family = poisson(link = "log"))

lmtest::lrtest(state_poi_mod, global_poi_mod)

```

### Table of ATE estimates by department

```{r}
#| label: department-ate-table

dist_summ %>%
  arrange(ATE) %>%
  dplyr::select(district, ends_with("_Treatment"), ends_with("_Control"), ATE_CI) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

```

Mortality rates are in deaths per 1000 person-years among children aged 1-59 months. ATE = mean mortality rate in treatment group - mean mortality rate in control group, by department. Negative ATEs are favorable.

The ATE estimates vary meaningfully across departments, with most showing reductions in mortality under treatment. ATEs ranged from `r round(min(dept_ate), 1)`^★^ (Gaya; control rate `r round(dept_mort_ctrl[["Gaya"]], 1)`^★^, treatment rate `r round(dept_mort_trt[["Gaya"]], 1)`^★^ deaths per 1,000 person-years) to `r round(max(dept_ate), 1)`^★^ deaths per 1,000 person-years (Boboye; control rate `r round(dept_mort_ctrl[["Boboye"]], 1)`^★^, treatment rate `r round(dept_mort_trt[["Boboye"]], 1)`^★^), indicating heterogeneity in intervention effectiveness. Notably, Boboye is the only department with a positive ATE (`r round(dept_ate[["Boboye"]], 1)`^★^ deaths per 1,000 person-years), which warrants further investigation.

```{r}
#| label: ate-ci-plot

dist_summ %>%
  arrange(desc(ATE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = reorder(district, desc(ATE_mean)), x = ATE_mean)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = ATE_CI_low, xmax = ATE_CI_high), width = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 0), linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(y = "Department", x = "Average Treatment Effect (deaths per 1000 py)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_blank())

```

### Test of heterogeneity in ATE across departments

```{r}
#| label: heterogeneity-test-ate

state_poi_mod <- glm(n_deaths_1to59 ~ isTreated_child + factor(district) + offset(log(pt_year_1to59)),
                      data = subset(df_all, pt_year_1to59 > 0), family = poisson(link = "log"))

tx_state_poi_mod <- glm(n_deaths_1to59 ~ isTreated_child * factor(district) + offset(log(pt_year_1to59)),
                        data = subset(df_all, pt_year_1to59 > 0), family = poisson(link = "log"))

lmtest::lrtest(tx_state_poi_mod, state_poi_mod)

```

```{r}
data_mort_control <- base_map +

data_mort_control | data_mort_treat | data_mort_ate
```

### Boboye's positive ATE

Boboye is the only department with a positive ATE (higher mortality in treatment than control), so we look more closely at the spatial distribution of outcomes within that department.

```{r}
#| label: boboye-maps
#| fig-width: 10
```

The positive ATE does not seem to be driven by a few outliers with high mortality in the treatment group, but rather a general shift in the distribution of mortality rates across the department. Boboye also has the lowest overall mortality rates in the control arm and was also part of MORDOR and hence given MDA for an extended period of time, which may be related to the positive ATE.

# Spatial models

We fit four Poisson generalized linear mixed models accounting for spatial correlation through a Matérn-structured random effect to predict mortality rates across the study area. The models are:

1.  *Simple kriging model*: Has a Matern correlation structure and a binary treatment indicator and no covariates (simp_krig)
2.  *Generalized (Universal) kriging model*: Has a Matern correlation structure, a binary treatment indicator, and linear terms for latitude and longitude as covariates (gen_krig)
3.  *Generalized kriging model with interaction between treatment indicator and lat/lon terms*: Has a Matern correlation structure, a binary treatment indicator, linear terms for latitude and longitude as covariates, and an interaction between the treatment indicator and the linear lat/lon terms (gen_krig_int)
4.  *Generalized kriging model with a site-specific random effect*: Has a Matern correlation structure, a binary treatment indicator, linear terms for latitude and longitude as covariates, and a random effect term for grappe (gen_krig_re)

All models included an offset for log person-years of follow-up and were fit using the `spaMM::fitme()` function. We then used the fitted models to predict mortality rates across a grid of locations covering the study area and compared the predictions across models and treatment groups. We also used the predicted mortality rates to estimate the ATE across the study area and compared the spatial distribution of ATE estimates across models.

## Model comparison

```{r}
#| label: model-comparison

aics %>%
  arrange(AIC) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

lrts %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

```

## Matern correlations

```{r}

knitr::include_graphics(c(
  here::here("results", "figs", "matern_corrs.png")
))

```

From the above correlation plots, we see that the simple kriging model has a much longer range (`r round(range_simp_km, 1)`^★^ km) and slower decay than the generalized kriging models (range: `r round(range_gen_km, 1)`^★^ km for the base generalized kriging model). This is likely because the larger spatial range in the simple kriging model is trying to account for spatial variation that could be explained by the lat/lon covariates in the generalized kriging models. Based on a LRT (χ² = `r round(lrt_gen_vs_simp_stat, 2)`^★^, p = `r formatC(lrt_gen_vs_simp_p, format = "f", digits = 3)`^★^) and AIC values (simple kriging: `r round(aic_simp, 1)`^★^; generalized kriging: `r round(aic_gen, 1)`^★^), the generalized kriging models all outperformed the simple kriging model.

Based on LRT (χ² = `r round(lrt_int_vs_gen_stat, 2)`^★^, p = `r formatC(lrt_int_vs_gen_p, format = "f", digits = 3)`^★^) and AIC values (generalized + interaction: `r round(aic_gen_int, 1)`^★^; generalized only: `r round(aic_gen, 1)`^★^; generalized + RE: `r round(aic_gen_re, 1)`^★^), the generalized kriging model with interaction was preferred. The estimated spatial range for the selected model was `r round(range_gen_int_km, 1)`^★^ km (Matérn ν = `r round(nu_gen_krig_int, 3)`^★^, λ = `r round(lambda_gen_int, 3)`^★^). The similarity in correlation structures across the generalized models suggests that adding interaction terms or random effects does not substantially change the scale of spatial dependence, but instead refines how spatial variation is partitioned between fixed effects and residual spatial structure.

*NOTE* The "range" in these plots is just the inverse of the rho parameter in the matern correlation. We could use alternative definitions of range that might be more interpretable, such as the distance at which correlation drops to 0.1, for example.

## Mortality predictions from spatial models

```{r}
#| label: model-predictions
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 10

pred_long <- ate_preds %>%
  dplyr::select(-ATE) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(predControl, predTreatment), names_to = "tx_group", values_to = "pred")

grouped <- pred_long %>%
  group_by(model, tx_group) %>%
  group_split()

group_keys <- pred_long %>%
  group_by(model, tx_group) %>%
  group_keys()

results <- purrr::map(grouped, ~
  make_raster_map(.x, proj_crs, global_crs, "pred")
)

names(results) <- paste(group_keys$model, group_keys$tx_group, sep = "__")

raster_df <- imap_dfr(results, function(res, name) {
  
  # parse names like "gen_krige__Treatment"
  model <- strsplit(name, "__")[[1]][1]
  tx_group <- strsplit(name, "__")[[1]][2]
  
  as.data.frame(res, xy = TRUE, na.rm = FALSE) %>%
    mutate(
      model = model,
      tx_group = tx_group
    )
})

raster_df$model <- factor(raster_df$model, 
levels = c("simp_krig", "gen_krig", "gen_krig_int", "gen_krig_re"),
labels = c("Simple", "Gen", "Gen + int", "Gen + RE"),
ordered = TRUE)

raster_df$tx_group <- factor(raster_df$tx_group,
levels = c("predTreatment", "predControl"),
labels = c("Treatment", "Control"),
ordered = TRUE)

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = raster_df, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = pred), na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_sf(data = niger_adm2, fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 0.25) +
  facet_grid(tx_group ~ model) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  annotation_scale() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
  axis.title = element_blank()) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 35),
                      na.value = NA,
                      breaks = seq(0,30,by=10),
                      guide=guide_colorbar(title="Modeled mortality rate (per 1000 person-years)", 
                                          title.position = "top",
                                          title.hjust = 0.5,
                                          label.position = "bottom",
                                          label.hjust = 0.5,
                                          barheight=unit(10,"pt"),
                                          barwidth=unit(200,"pt"),
                                          ticks.colour = "white",
                                          ticks.linewidth = 1,
                                          frame.colour = "white")) +
  scale_y_continuous(n.breaks = 5) +
  scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 3)

ggsave(here("results", "figs", "model_mort_pred.png"),
bg = "white",
width = 8, height = 6, units = "in")

```

The predicted mortality surfaces are visually similar across models, with consistent large-scale spatial patterns and only subtle differences in local variation (evidenced in the scatter plots below). This suggests that the larger spatial signal is captured even by simpler generalized kriging models.

```{r compare predictions}

  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +

gen_re_corr_plot <- ggplot(data = pred_model_wide, aes(x = gen_krig, y = gen_krig_re, group = tx_group, color = tx_group)) +
```

The high correlations between model predictions confirm that all models produce very similar estimates across the spatial domain. The simple kriging model shows slightly more deviation, consistent with its longer-range correlation structure and lack of covariates. The generalized models are nearly indistinguishable in their predictions, indicating that additional model complexity yields only marginal changes in fitted values.

The generalized kriging model with interaction is the only model that clearly captures a localized positive ATE in Boboye. This suggests that allowing the treatment effect to vary with spatial covariates (latitude/longitude) is necessary to detect region-specific reversals in effect direction.     )

```{r}
  geom_sf(data = niger_adm2, fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 0.25) +

  axis.title = element_blank()) +
  scale_fill_viridis(option = "magma", direction = 1,
                      limits = c(0.3, 1),
                      na.value = NA,
                      # breaks = seq(0,10,by=2),
                      guide = guide_colorbar(title="Posterior pr(mortality ATE < 0)",  
                                          title.position = "top",
                                          title.hjust = 0.5,
                                          label.position = "bottom",
                                          label.hjust = 0.5,
                                          barheight=unit(10,"pt"),
                                          barwidth=unit(200,"pt"),
                                          ticks.colour = "white",
                                          ticks.linewidth = 1,
                                          frame.colour = "white")) +
  scale_y_continuous(n.breaks = 5) +
  scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 3)

ggsave(here("results", "figs", "model_posterior_prob_map.png"),
bg = "white",
width = 8, height = 6, units = "in")

```

The posterior probability map provides a probabilistic interpretation of treatment benefit. Areas with high probability (close to 1) indicate strong evidence that treatment reduces mortality, while lower values indicate uncertainty or potential harm. Compared to the base generalized model, the interaction model produces more spatially differentiated probability surfaces, particularly in regions like Boboye, where the probability of benefit is substantially lower. This reinforces the conclusion that treatment effects are spatially heterogeneous.

This was estimated using a simulation-based approach where we drew samples from the posterior distribution of model parameters, calculated the ATE for each sample, and then computed the proportion of samples where the ATE was less than 0 at each location. This approach accounts for uncertainty in model parameters and provides a more nuanced assessment of treatment effects across space.

# CSI-level analysis

We also fit spatial models at the CSI level, which has less spatial granularity than the grappe-level data but may still capture some spatial correlation. The `r n_csis`^★^ CSIs had a median of `r csi_med_deaths`^★^ deaths per CSI (range: `r csi_min_deaths`–`r csi_max_deaths`^★^) and a median of `r scales::comma(csi_med_pt)`^★^ person-years per CSI (range: `r scales::comma(csi_min_pt)`–`r scales::comma(csi_max_pt)`^★^). Since the randomization was at the grappe level, we cannot include a term for the treatment indicator in the CSI-level models, but we can still fit spatial models to predict mortality rates across the study area and compare the spatial correlation structure to the grappe-level models, akin to how it will be done in future programmatic surveillance analyses.

```{r}
})

csi_raster_df$model <- factor(csi_raster_df$model,

ordered = TRUE)

ggplot() +

                      na.value = NA,

                      guide=guide_colorbar(title="Modeled mortality rate (per 1000 person-years)", 
                                          title.position = "top",
                                          title.hjust = 0.5,
                                          label.position = "bottom",
                                          label.hjust = 0.5,
                                          barheight=unit(10,"pt"),
                                          barwidth=unit(200,"pt"),
                                          ticks.colour = "white",

# <!-- When comparing this csi-level aggregate analysis to the grappe-level analysis, we see that the csi-level models have a larger Matern correlation range (`r round(range_csi_km, 2)`^★^ km for the generalized kriging model) compared to the grappe-level models (range of `r round(range_gen_km, 2)`^★^ km for the generalized kriging model and `r round(range_gen_int_km, 2)`^★^ km when we include an interaction with treatment). This suggests that there is more spatial correlation in the grappe-level data than in the csi-level data, which makes sense given that the grappe-level data has more spatial granularity and may capture more local spatial patterns. -->

```

Despite the loss of spatial resolution, the CSI-level analysis preserves the broad spatial gradients in mortality. However, the increased correlation range suggests that aggregation smooths over local variability, effectively inflating the apparent spatial scale of dependence. This implies that CSI-level surveillance may be adequate for identifying large-scale patterns but may miss localized hotspots or heterogeneity in treatment effects that are detectable at the grappe level.

# Variance partitioning

Using a model with treatment indicator, matern correlation, and a random effect for district and csi nested in district, we partition the variance in mortality rates (on the latent scale) into components attributable to treatment, spatial correlation (sub-csi level variance), district-level effects, and csi-level effects.

The variance partitioning results suggest that approximately 97.6% of the variance in mortality is explained by fine-scale spatial correlation, 2.4% is explained by differences between CSIs within districts, and 0% is explained by differences between districts.
